title: Extract a list of all employee names from the employee list.
shortTitle: Extract a list of all employee names from the employee list

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is the canonical `map` transformation. `Stream.map(Function)` applies a one-argument function to every element, producing a new stream of the transformed values. Extracting names is `stream.map(Employee::getName)`, turning a stream of `Employee` into a stream of `String`, which you collect into a list.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR clerk at the National Bank of India has a stack of full employee files but the manager only wants a printed list of names. She goes through each file and copies just the name onto a fresh sheet. `map` is that act of pulling one piece out of each item to build a new, simpler list.

**One line to remember:** `map` transforms each element into something else, one in and one out, producing a new stream of the results.

sections.s2_technical:
The `map` method takes a `Function<T, R>`, a functional interface whose single method `R apply(T t)` converts one value into another. For name extraction the function takes an `Employee` and returns its name `String`, so `map` changes the stream's element type from `Employee` to `String`. The relationship is strictly one-to-one: every input produces exactly one output, so the output stream has the same number of elements as the input.

You can write the function as a lambda `e -> e.getName()` or, more concisely, as a method reference `Employee::getName`. The method reference is preferred when it simply calls an existing method, because it is shorter and signals intent clearly without the ceremony of a lambda parameter.

After mapping you need a terminal operation to materialise the result. `collect(Collectors.toList())` gathers the names into a `List<String>`. On Java 16 and later `toList()` directly on the stream returns an unmodifiable list, which is a slightly cleaner alternative when you do not need to mutate the result.

A senior nuance: `map` is one-to-one and does not flatten. If your function returned a collection per element you would get a stream of collections, which is where `flatMap` comes in. Keeping the distinction clear — map for one-to-one, flatMap for one-to-many — is a frequent interview discriminator.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's branch manager wants a simple roll-call sheet for a staff meeting: just the names, not the whole employee record with salary and department. The HR system stores rich employee objects, but the meeting only needs a flat list of names. This is exactly how map works — each full employee is transformed into just its name, producing a clean list of strings.

The code defines an `Employee` with name, department and salary. A `RosterService` exposes `allNames(List<Employee>)` using map with a method reference. The runnable `Main` feeds the staff list and logs the extracted names.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three Employee objects — Rajesh (IT, 95000), Priya (Sales, 72000), Amit (HR, 48000).

Step 1: The stream opens over three rich employee objects.

Step 2: Rajesh flows into map. The function getName pulls out the string Rajesh, so the stream now carries the string Rajesh instead of the full object.

Step 3: Priya flows in and becomes the string Priya.

Step 4: Amit flows in and becomes the string Amit.

Step 5: The element type of the stream is now String, not Employee, and there are still exactly three elements because map is one-to-one.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the three strings into a list of names.

```

INFO: Extracting names from 3 employees
Oct 30, 2026 11:25:03 AM com.bank.roster.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Roll call: [Rajesh, Priya, Amit]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Stream<Employee> [Rajesh{IT,95k}, Priya{Sales,72k}, Amit{HR,48k}]
    │
    ▼
  map(Employee::getName)        (type changes Employee → String)
    ├─ Rajesh{...} → "Rajesh"
    ├─ Priya{...}  → "Priya"
    └─ Amit{...}   → "Amit"
    │  (still 3 elements — one-to-one)
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  List<String> ["Rajesh","Priya","Amit"]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To extract one field out of each object I use the map operation, which applies a function to every element and produces a new stream of the transformed values. For names I map with a function that takes an employee and returns its name, which changes the stream's element type from employee to string, and then I collect the result into a list. Because map is strictly one-to-one, the output list has exactly the same number of elements as the input.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was a staff roll-call sheet for a branch meeting. The HR system stores rich employee objects with salary and department, but the meeting only needed a flat list of names, so I streamed the employees and mapped each one to just its name. I used a method reference rather than a full lambda because it simply calls an existing getter, which is shorter and signals the intent clearly.

A senior point I always make is the distinction between map and flatMap. Map is one-to-one, so each input yields exactly one output and nothing is flattened. If my function had returned a collection for each element I would end up with a stream of collections, and that is exactly where flatMap is needed to flatten one-to-many relationships into a single stream. Keeping that boundary clear in my head prevents a very common mistake. I also note that on newer Java I can call the terminal toList directly on the stream to get an unmodifiable list when I do not need to mutate the result.
